Every Spenserian stanza has nine lines..why: The definition of the stanza (eight lines of iambic pentameter and a closing alexandrine, rhymed ababbcbcc), stated in every handbook of verse and in the Wikipedia article. No exceptions: a stanza of another length is not called Spenserian.

sources.quote: Each stanza contains nine lines in total

Keats's The Eve of St. Agnes is written.why: The poem's form is named with it in reference texts and its Wikipedia lead. Its stanza length is rarely stated by name, so the by-name worlds (w1, w3) are the weaker ones here.

notes: TBox rule edit, re-picked in review: the writer's rule (every Old English poem is written in alliterative verse) had no consistent by-name world, because 'Beowulf is an Old English poem' is entailed by its language, a firm fact, so Beowulf cannot leave the class and the background-belief queries were really determinate. Here membership is defined by the stanza's shape, so a poem whose stanza length is stored by name can leave the class: in the by-name worlds its nine-line stanzas stop being Spenserian; the poem is never an exception to the rule. The Faerie Queene is not used as a member: the stanza is named after it, so its membership cannot give way. Derivability very_unlikely: the definition of the stanza. No exceptions. Plausibility: the first eight lines are the pentameter body of the stanza, and ottava rima has eight lines; clearly false. New members are invented poems named in the prompt. Well-known members: Keats's The Eve of St. Agnes and Shelley's Adonais, both written entirely in Spenserian stanzas (Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage is avoided: it includes lyrics in other forms). Two independent storage choices, four worlds; the rule worlds are likelier (Decisions 4). R4 risk: smaller models may not know the stanza's length. Near query: The Faerie Queene's author, which shares the subject and whose answer differs from the new one (R6). Chinese: 斯宾塞诗节 names the poet, not the length.
